analysis.one_liner: Bars the president from pausing quarterly oil and gas lease sales on federal land.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate Energy Committee with just 2 Republican sponsors until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write into law that the president cannot pause the quarterly onshore oil and gas lease sales that federal law requires the Interior Department to hold. It targets President Biden's January 2021 climate executive order, which had paused new leasing while it was reviewed. If any sale was canceled or delayed because of that order, the bill would force Interior to hold a replacement sale within two years. [S2][S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that bid on federal leases would get a guaranteed schedule of quarterly onshore lease sales that no president could pause, plus replacement sales to make up for any sales lost to the 2021 pause. States that collect revenue from federal drilling, like Utah, would also benefit. [S2][S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies leasing federal land

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit the president from pausing or preventing the quarterly onshore lease sales required by the Mineral Leasing Act, so lease sales would continue regardless of any executive order.

It would require the Interior Department to hold a replacement lease sale within two years of any sale canceled, delayed, or paused because of Executive Order 14008, making companies whole for sales lost during the 2021 pause.
By locking in a fixed leasing schedule, it would remove the uncertainty created by the January 2021 leasing pause for companies planning drilling on federal land.

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the cost in the form of continued oil and gas extraction on federal land even when a president judged a pause necessary for climate or other reasons, since the bill strips that authority. Any environmental review or market condition that would otherwise justify delaying a sale could not stop the schedule. [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through continued federal-land extraction

drawbacks.text: The bill would take away a president's authority to pause federal leasing for climate reasons, handcuffing the executive branch even if a future administration or Congress judged the leasing program harmful.

It would mandate quarterly lease sales 'notwithstanding any other provision of law,' meaning the leasing schedule could not be adjusted for changing circumstances, court rulings, or environmental findings.

Supporters would argue the 2021 leasing pause contributed to high gasoline prices and greater reliance on foreign oil, and that the quarterly sales were already required by existing law, so the bill merely enforced the status quo.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is limited: quarterly onshore lease sales were already required by law, so the bill mainly removed the president's ability to pause them. The cost is a permanent loss of executive flexibility over public-land energy policy, which matters most for climate and land management. The benefit to consumers at the gas pump is speculative and small, since federal leasing changes affect supply slowly, while the loss of flexibility is real and lasting.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Lee introduced the bill on July 20, 2022, with Senator Rick Scott as its only cosponsor.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee the same day; that was its last action.
The committee never held a hearing or a vote, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 with the bill still parked there.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies gained nothing, since they did not get the guaranteed lease schedule they sought. The administration kept whatever authority existing law and the courts left it over federal leasing, and no new mandate to hold quarterly sales was added.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The administration; oil companies gained nothing new

for.name: Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip the president's authority to pause federal onshore lease sales.

for.name: Rick Scott
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only additional sponsor it attracted.

for.name: Oil and gas industry groups
for.what_they_did: Pushed to reverse or limit the 2021 federal leasing pause during the energy price spike.

against.name: Joe Manchin
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it sat in his committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Only 2 of 50 Senate Republicans backed the bill as sponsor or cosponsor, no Democrat or independent supported it, and it never reached a vote where the chamber's party split (48 D, 2 I, 50 R) could have been tested.

industries.note: The bill would have guaranteed a steady quarterly schedule of federal onshore lease sales and replacement sales for anything lost to the 2021 pause, giving companies more certainty and access to public-land drilling. The public upside is at most cheaper energy down the road; the public cost is more extraction and emissions from federal land and less executive flexibility to manage it.

industries.industry: States and counties with federal drilling revenue
industries.note: States like Utah share in royalties from federal leases, so mandated lease sales would keep that revenue flowing. This benefit depends entirely on continued federal extraction.
